subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 22-year-old man presents with 3 days of dysuria and a purulent urethral discharge. He is afebrile and has no rash. A urethral smear shows neutrophils containing intracellular gram-negative diplococci. He reports a new sexual partner 2 weeks ago and has never been tested for sexually transmitted infections.
question: Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
explanation_correct: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus that is often seen intracellularly within neutrophils and produces IgA proteases. It is sexually and perinatally transmitted and causes gonorrhea, septic arthritis, neonatal conjunctivitis at 2 to 5 days after birth, pelvic inflammatory disease, and Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome, and it is diagnosed with NAAT.

explanation_incorrect.B: Chlamydia trachomatis causes nongonococcal urethritis, but it is an obligate intracellular organism that does not stain on Gram as gram-negative diplococci and characteristically produces cytoplasmic inclusions.
explanation_incorrect.C: Treponema pallidum is a spirochete visualized by dark-field or fluorescent microscopy and produces a painless chancre, not a purulent urethral discharge.
explanation_incorrect.D: Escherichia coli is a lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod causing urinary tract infection, not a diplococcus seen inside neutrophils in urethral discharge.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neisseria meningitidis is also a gram-negative diplococcus but is transmitted by respiratory and oral secretions and causes meningococcemia and meningitis rather than urethritis.

educationalObjective: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is an intracellular gram-negative diplococcus in neutrophils causing urethritis, PID, and neonatal conjunctivitis.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 24-year-old woman presents with 5 days of lower abdominal pain, fever, and purulent vaginal discharge. She has worsening pain in the right upper quadrant with pleuritic features on inspiration. Pelvic examination shows cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness, and NAAT of a vaginal swab is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
question: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of the right upper quadrant pain in this patient?

options.text: Inflammation of the liver capsule and adjacent peritoneum
Liver abscess from portal vein bacteremia

explanation_correct: This is Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome, in which gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease spreads within the peritoneum to produce inflammation of the liver capsule, causing right upper quadrant pleuritic pain. Gonococci cause PID and Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome in addition to urethritis, septic arthritis, and neonatal conjunctivitis at 2 to 5 days after birth.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ascending biliary infection in the setting of obstruction typically involves enteric organisms such as E coli and would present with jaundice and cholestasis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Gonococcal endocarditis is rare and causes valvular findings and systemic emboli, not isolated perihepatic pain following pelvic infection.
explanation_incorrect.D: A liver abscess would show a focal fluid collection rather than thin adhesions between the liver capsule and diaphragm, and it is not the classic complication described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Gallbladder seeding would not be expected from an ascending genital infection and would produce focal gallbladder findings rather than perihepatic inflammation after PID.

educationalObjective: Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis complicating gonococcal or chlamydial PID and produces right upper quadrant pleuritic pain.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 23-year-old man is diagnosed with uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis. He is treated with a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone. The clinic's molecular testing for chlamydial coinfection has not yet resulted, and the clinician is deciding whether to add additional antibiotics. The team also discusses why there is no gonococcal vaccine.
question: Which of the following best explains the current approach to treatment and prevention in this patient?

options.text: Treat with single-dose ceftriaxone and add doxycycline if chlamydial coinfection is not excluded, since no vaccine exists because of antigenic variation of pilus proteins
Manage with erythromycin eye ointment alone
Immunize with a polysaccharide conjugate vaccine after treatment
Use penicillin G monotherapy because resistance is not described
Provide rifampin prophylaxis to all sexual contacts without treating the patient

explanation_correct: Gonorrhea is treated with a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone, and if chlamydial coinfection has not been excluded by molecular testing, doxycycline is added. No gonococcal vaccine exists because of antigenic variation of pilus proteins, unlike meningococcus, for which a vaccine is available. Condoms reduce sexual transmission, and erythromycin eye ointment in the newborn prevents neonatal blindness.

explanation_incorrect.B: Erythromycin eye ointment is a neonatal preventive measure against ophthalmia neonatorum, not a treatment for established adult urethritis.
explanation_incorrect.C: There is no gonococcal vaccine because pilus proteins vary antigenically, so vaccination is not part of management.
explanation_incorrect.D: Penicillin G monotherapy is the treatment for syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum, not for gonorrhea, and gonococcal penicillin resistance is well recognized.
explanation_incorrect.E: Rifampin prophylaxis for contacts applies to meningococcal and Haemophilus disease; the patient himself requires antibiotic treatment for gonorrhea.

educationalObjective: Gonorrhea is treated with single-dose IM ceftriaxone plus doxycycline if chlamydia is not excluded, and no vaccine exists due to pilus antigenic variation.
